title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights, citing customer-data and loyalty risk
subtitle: The carrier amended its Contract of Carriage to prohibit any purchase, change, or servicing of tickets by AI agents — even with a passenger's supervision — and reserved the right to cancel such reservations without notice. Delta and American say they are still evaluating.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: United Airlines updated its Contract of Carriage effective November 11 to prohibit third-party AI agents from booking, modifying, or servicing tickets on United. The ban covers United's website and app, travel agency channels, and ancillary purchases such as seats and upgrades. A new Rule 5.H lets United cancel 'reservations made, modified or serviced by AI Agents' without notice. The policy applies even when a passenger is supervising the agent or approves its actions. Agents remain free to display United fares in comparison tools such as Kayak, Hopper, and Google Flights. Delta and American told Fast Company they allow some AI tools to transact on their systems today and are continuing to evaluate the landscape.

United's stated rationale is customer-data protection, loyalty-account security, and federal aviation compliance. The operative constraint behind those stated reasons is distribution economics. Airlines spent a decade fighting to pull consumers back into direct channels and away from online travel agencies that captured margin and the customer relationship. A generation of autonomous booking agents would re-intermediate that relationship through whichever model vendor controls the agent — and United's CEO Scott Kirby has been explicit in interviews that he does not want 'another middleman.' Enforcement is the open question: contract language is not detection, and United's claim that its systems can identify booking sources will be tested in practice.

The move arrives as the browser-agent category hits its first real wave of commercial friction. Banks and large retailers have already restricted agent access on similar grounds. OpenAI's agent mode, Anthropic's Claude for Chrome, and Google's Gemini computer-use features have all shipped in the last six months, and a growing list of counterparties is refusing to transact with them. Expect a split where companies that compete for direct customer relationships — airlines, banks, insurers — resist, while commoditized intermediaries that already lost the customer relationship open up fast to stay relevant.

A takeaway for learners: the economics of AI agents are being set by terms of service, not by model capability. If you are building on top of a browser-agent stack, read the target site's Terms of Service and Contract of Carriage before you ship — a technically capable workflow that the counterparty prohibits is a liability, not a product. If you are studying the agent economy, the list of companies banning agents is a better leading indicator of where the real value sits than the list of companies deploying them.
